entry: Member of the learned class of the ancient [[Celts|Celtic]] peoples of [[Gaul]] and the [[British Isles]]. Classical writers described druids as priests, teachers, judges and custodians of religious and legal tradition, but because they committed nothing to writing, most knowledge of them comes from outside observers. They were credited with teaching the immortality of the soul. Druids declined after the Roman conquest of Gaul and faced imperial prohibitions in the 1st century CE. The familiar image of white robes, oak groves and mistletoe derives largely from a single passage by [[Pliny the Elder]].

[[Percussion instrument]] with a membrane, or drumhead, stretched over a shell and struck by hand, stick or mallet. In the Hornbostel–Sachs system drums are membranophones. They are among the world's oldest and most ubiquitous [[Musical instrument|musical instruments]], and their basic design has remained virtually unchanged for thousands of years. Some drums, such as the [[Djembe|djembe]], are almost always played singly, while bongo drums and timpani are played in sets by one player. A number of drums together with [[Cymbal|cymbals]] form the basic modern drum kit. In [[Jazz|jazz]], some drummers use brushes for a smoother, quieter sound. Drums often have symbolic roles in religious ceremonies and are used in music therapy because of their tactile nature. In Burundi the karyenda drum was a symbol of royal power.

Esoteric ethnoreligious group of the [[Levant]]. The Druze call themselves al-Muwaḥḥidūn ("the monotheists"). Their faith developed from the Ismāʿīli branch of Shiʿa [[Islam]] and teaches the unity of God, [[Reincarnation|reincarnation]] and the eternity of the [[Soul|soul]]. Druze do not identify as Muslims, maintain the Arabic language and culture, and keep most practices secret; conversion is not permitted. The *Epistles of Wisdom* is the central text. Druze number between 800,000 and a million, mainly in [[Lebanon]], [[Syria]] and [[Israel]], with smaller communities in [[Jordan]]. The Arabian hypothesis, the most widely accepted theory of origin among historians and within the community, holds that they descend from 12 Arab tribes that migrated to Syria. The Druze have often faced religious persecution.

Basin or depression that formerly contained a standing surface water body, which disappears when [[Evaporation|evaporation]] exceeds recharge. It is also called a playa. Dry lakes form when water collects in a depression and then evaporates, leaving dissolved [[Salt|salts]] that build up over time. If the floor is covered by alkaline compounds it is an alkali flat; if covered with salt, a salt flat. Dry lakes are typically found in semi-arid to arid regions. The largest concentration, nearly 22,000, lies in the southern High Plains of Texas and eastern New Mexico. Salar de Uyuni in [[Bolivia]], the largest salt flat in the world, covers 10,582 sq km. On the Racetrack Playa in [[Death Valley]], California, wind-driven ice sheets move rocks known as "sailing stones", which move only once every two or three years.

Yearly period of low rainfall, especially in the [[Tropics|tropics]]. The tropical rain belt moves between the northern and southern tropics over the year, so the dry season falls in the northern tropics from about November to March and in the southern tropics from May to September. At the equator there are two wet and two dry seasons. Under the [[Köppen climate classification]], a tropical dry-season month has average precipitation below 60 mm (2.4 in). Humidity is low, watering holes and rivers dry up, and grazing animals such as [[Zebra|zebras]], [[Elephant|elephants]] and [[Wildebeest|wildebeest]] move to more fertile areas. Bushfires, or [[Wildfire|wildfires]], are common. In Africa the start of the dry season coincides with a rise in [[Measles|measles]] cases, as farmers move into cities and population density increases.

American materials company headquartered in [[Delaware]]. Founded in 1802 by French-American chemist Éleuthère Irénée du Pont de Nemours as a gunpowder maker, it became the largest supplier of gunpowder to the U.S. military by the mid-19th century, providing one-third to one-half of the powder used by the Union army in the [[American Civil War]]. It began producing [[Dynamite|dynamite]] in the 1880s. Its 20th-century polymers include [[Nylon]], Teflon and [[Kevlar]]. DuPont merged with the Dow Chemical Company in 2017 and later reverted to its own name. Lawsuits and settlements followed [[PFAS]] contamination linked to PFOA used in Teflon manufacturing.

[[Tang dynasty|Tang]] dynasty Chinese poet and government official. With his older contemporary and friend [[Li Bai]], he is one of the principal poets associated with Tang poetry, and nearly 1,500 poems attributed to him survive. He pursued an official career and briefly served as a remonstrance official at the imperial court. The [[An Lushan rebellion]], which began in 755, displaced him and his family and shaped much of his later writing. He lived in Qinzhou and [[Chengdu]] before traveling through the middle [[Yangtze]] region. Accounts differ on the place and cause of his death. Later Chinese critics called him the "Poet-Historian" and the "Poet-Sage". His poetry records war, displacement, official life and everyday observation, and influenced Chinese and Japanese literary traditions.

Most populous city of the [[United Arab Emirates]], on the southeastern coast of the [[Persian Gulf]] (pop., 2025: 4 million). Founded in the early 18th century as a pearling and fishing settlement, Dubai became a regional trade hub after declaring itself a free port in 1901 and extending its creek in 1961. Oil revenue accelerated development from the 1960s to the 1990s, but in 2018 oil production contributed less than 1% of GDP. Rapid construction since the 1990s produced one of the world's densest skylines, including the [[Burj Khalifa]], the world's tallest building. Land reclamation has added more than 300 km of artificial coastline. The economy centers on trade, tourism, aviation, financial services and real estate. [[Dubai International Airport]] is the world's busiest airport for international passenger traffic.

Primary international airport of [[Dubai]], [[United Arab Emirates]], identified by the code DXB. It was the world's busiest airport by international passenger traffic in 2025, handling over 95.2 million passengers that year. [[Emirates (airline)|Emirates]] operates its main hub, handling 51% of passenger traffic, and Terminal 3 is the largest airport terminal in the world. The airport is planned to close once the expanded Al Maktoum International Airport is fully operational.

Capital and largest city of [[Ireland]]. Situated on Dublin Bay at the mouth of the River Liffey, it lies in the province of Leinster. The city council area had a population of 592,713 at the 2022 census, and the city including suburbs had 1,263,219. A Gaelic settlement existed by the 7th century, followed by a [[Vikings|Viking]] settlement of about 841. Dublin became Ireland's principal settlement by the 12th century, after the Anglo-Norman invasion. It was briefly the second-largest city in the [[British Empire]] after the Acts of Union in 1800. Following independence in 1922 it became the capital of the Irish Free State, renamed Ireland in 1937. Global firms including [[Google]] and [[Microsoft]] have headquarters there.

Coastal city in southern Dalmatia, [[Croatia]], on the [[Adriatic Sea|Adriatic]]. Known historically as Ragusa, it was probably founded in the 7th century by refugees from Epidaurum. It was under Byzantine protection and later under the [[Republic of Venice]]. Between the 14th and 19th centuries it ruled itself as a free state, its prosperity based on maritime trade. Dubrovnik became a cradle of Croatian literature. A 1667 earthquake almost destroyed the entire city. [[UNESCO]] inscribed its Old City as a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1979. In 1991, during the [[Croatian War of Independence]], the Yugoslav People's Army besieged the city for seven months.

Medieval and early modern feudal polity of north-western historical Burgundy, part of the [[Kingdom of France]]. The first attested duke, Richard the Justiciar, held the title in 918. The Burgundian male line ended in 1361, and the duchy reverted to the Valois kings. In 1363 King John II ceded it to his younger son Philip, who through his marriage to Countess Margaret III of [[Flanders]] laid the foundation for a Burgundian state stretching from the western Alps to the North Sea. The last duke, Charles the Bold, was killed at the 1477 Battle of Nancy. King [[Louis XI]] then absorbed the duchy into the French crown lands, while the Low Countries passed to Charles's daughter Mary and her Habsburg descendants.

Common name for numerous species of waterfowl in the family Anatidae, roughly 170 species in all. Ducks are generally smaller and shorter-necked than [[Swan|swans]] and [[Goose|geese]], which belong to the same family, though the group is not monophyletic. The word comes from Old English dūce, "diver". Ducks are mostly aquatic and occur in fresh and sea water. Dabbling ducks, such as the [[Mallard]], feed by tipping up in shallow water, while diving ducks forage underwater. A male is called a drake and a female a duck or hen, and young ducks are called ducklings. Ducks are sometimes confused with [[Loon|loons]], grebes, moorhens and coots.

Arranged engagement in combat between two people with matched weapons, fought under a code of honor. Duels were mostly fought with swords, such as the [[Rapier]], in the 17th and 18th centuries, but from the late 18th century in England [[Pistol|pistols]] became more common. Participants sought "satisfaction", restoring their honor by demonstrating a willingness to risk their lives, rather than killing the opponent. Dueling was reserved for male members of the nobility and later extended to the upper classes. The Fourth Council of the Lateran (1215) outlawed duels, and from the early 17th century they became illegal where practiced. Dueling declined in England by the mid-19th century and in Continental Europe by the turn of the 20th century. In the United States it waned before the American Civil War; public opinion, not legislation, caused the change. The 1804 duel between [[Alexander Hamilton]] and [[Aaron Burr]] was fatal.

Herbivorous marine mammal, the only living member of the family Dugongidae. It is one of four living species of the order [[Sirenia]], alongside three [[Manatee|manatees]]. The dugong feeds on seagrass in shallow coastal waters across the Indo-West Pacific, from [[East Africa]] to northern Australia. Its closest relative, [[Steller's sea cow]], was hunted to extinction in the 18th century. The IUCN lists the dugong as vulnerable, and fishing-related deaths, habitat degradation and hunting threaten it. With a lifespan of 70 years or more and slow reproduction, it is especially vulnerable to extinction.

American [[Jazz|jazz]] pianist, composer and bandleader. He led his jazz orchestra from 1924 for the rest of his life, and music critic Ralph J. Gleason called him "America's most important composer". Born in [[Washington, D.C.]], he was based in [[New York City]] from the mid-1920s and gained national prominence through his orchestra's appearances at the Cotton Club in Harlem. He wrote or collaborated on more than 1,000 compositions, many of which became standards. From the late 1930s he worked for nearly 30 years with the composer-arranger Billy Strayhorn. After a low-profile period, a July 1956 appearance at the Newport Jazz Festival led to a major revival and regular world tours. He received a posthumous Pulitzer Prize Special Award for music in 1999.

Private research university in Durham, [[North Carolina]]. Founded by [[Quakers|Quakers]] and Methodists in 1838, it moved to Durham in 1892. In 1924, after tobacco and electric power industrialist James Buchanan Duke established the Duke Endowment, the institution was renamed to honor his father, Washington Duke. The campus spans over 8,600 acres (3,500 hectares). In 2024 Duke spent more than $1.5 billion on research, and its $11.9 billion endowment ranks it as the twelfth-wealthiest private academic institution in the United States.

Broad class of dishes of cooked dough, often wrapped around a filling. The dough may be based on wheat or other flours, or on potatoes, and fillings include meat, fish, [[Tofu|tofu]], cheese or vegetables. Dumplings may be boiled, simmered, steamed, fried or baked, though some definitions exclude frying and baking to rule out fritters. The term entered English in the 17th century for a small lump of dough cooked by simmering or steaming. One of the earliest mentions is in a *fu* poem by the Chinese scholar Shu Xi around 300 CE, and archaeologically preserved dumplings from [[Xinjiang]], [[China]], date back over 1,000 years. Brazilian *pastéis* are thin dough stuffed with fillings such as ground beef or cheese, and Bajan dumplings are slightly sweetened.

Hill or ridge of wind- or water-driven sand. Dunes are most common in [[Desert|desert]] environments, where the lack of moisture limits vegetation, but they also form along shores, streams and in glacial outwash. Most dunes are longer on the stoss, or upflow, side and have a steeper slip face on the lee side. Five basic types are recognized: crescentic, linear, star, dome and parabolic. Barchan dunes are crescent-shaped, generally wider than they are long, and form under winds from one direction. The largest crescentic dunes, with mean crest-to-crest widths of more than 3 km, are in China's [[Taklamakan Desert]]. Coastal dunes help protect land against storm waves, and dune drift forced the Western Australian town of Eucla to be relocated in the 1890s.

American science fiction media franchise. It originated with the 1965 novel *Dune* by [[Frank Herbert]], which is frequently described as the best-selling science fiction novel in history and won the inaugural Nebula Award for Best Novel. Herbert wrote five sequels, and his son Brian Herbert and Kevin J. Anderson published further novels beginning in 1999. Adaptations include a 1984 film, a 2000 television miniseries and a two-part film adaptation released in 2021 and 2024. The franchise has also inspired tabletop games and video games. Since 2009, planet names from the novels have been adopted for features on [[Titan (moon)|Titan]], a moon of [[Saturn]].

Epic science fiction novel by American author [[Frank Herbert]], published in 1965. It was first serialized in *Analog* and tied with Roger Zelazny's *This Immortal* for the Hugo Award for Best Novel. It won the inaugural Nebula Award for Best Novel in 1966 and is the first installment of the Dune Chronicles. The story follows Paul Atreides, whose family takes stewardship of the desert planet Arrakis, the only source of the life-extending spice melange. As factions of the empire struggle for control of Arrakis, the novel explores politics, religion, ecology and technology. A 1984 film directed by [[David Lynch]] received mostly negative reviews, and a 2021 adaptation by Denis Villeneuve was nominated for ten [[Academy Awards]], winning six.

Informal group of [[Beetle|beetles]] that feed on feces. They belong to the superfamily Scarabaeoidea but are not a single taxonomic group, so dung feeding has evolved more than once. The subfamily Scarabaeinae alone comprises more than 5,000 species. Many feed on the dung of [[Herbivore|herbivores]] and omnivores, and they occur on every continent except [[Antarctica]]. In 1991 Ilkka Cambefort and Yves Hanski classified dung beetles as rollers, which shape dung into balls for food or brood, tunnelers, which bury dung where they find it, and dwellers, which live within dung. In the late 19th century Jean Henri Fabre showed that apparent helpers of a rolling beetle were waiting to steal its food. [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptians]] revered dung-rolling as the god Khepri rolling the sun across the sky.

Fantasy tabletop role-playing game, commonly abbreviated as D&D. Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson created it, and it was first published in 1974 by Tactical Studies Rules (TSR). Players create their own characters, while a Dungeon Master referees the game and voices the non-player characters. It is commonly recognized as the beginning of the modern role-playing game industry and deeply influenced [[Video game|video games]]. Sales of the fifth edition, released in 2014, rose another 52 percent in 2018. A 1980s moral panic attempted to link the game to [[Satanism]] and suicide.

Evacuation of Allied forces from the beaches and harbor of Dunkirk, northern France, in 1940. Codenamed Operation Dynamo, it took place between 26 May and 4 June 1940, and more than 338,000 Allied soldiers were evacuated. They had been trapped by German forces during the [[Battle of France]]. Royal Navy destroyers and a flotilla of over 800 vessels, including civilian "Little Ships", carried them to Britain. [[Winston Churchill|Churchill]] called the event "a colossal military disaster" but also hailed the "miracle of deliverance", adding that wars are not won by evacuations.

Extinct genus of large arthrodire ("jointed-neck") fishes. Members lived in the Late [[Devonian|Devonian]] period, about 382–358 million years ago, and were among the first vertebrate apex predators. Fossils have been found in the United States, Canada, Poland, [[Belgium]], [[Morocco]], Russia and Latvia. The type species, *Dunkleosteus terrelli*, is the largest and best known; typical adults are estimated at about 3.4 m long and exceptionally large individuals at 4.1 m. 10 species have been named, although the validity of several is unclear.
